name: protected access
desc: Visible in the same package and in subclasses anywhere. Wider than most beginners expect, narrower than public.
body: `protected` also exposes the field to every class in the same package, including code that is not a subclass. A `private` field with a `protected` getter gives subclasses read access without giving the whole package write access. Use `protected` for a value a subclass must read to do its job, and keep it `final` so the wider visibility cannot corrupt the object.

name: initialization order
desc: Static blocks run once per class, parent first. Instance blocks and constructors run on every object, top of the hierarchy first.
body: Static blocks run at first use, and the parent class is initialised before the child, so the parent block prints first. Per object the order is parent instance block, parent constructor body, child instance block, child constructor body. That order is why a method called from a parent constructor sees child fields at their default values, not at the values the child declares.

name: this(...) or super(...)
desc: Both must be the first statement of a constructor, so a constructor uses one or the other, never both.
body: A constructor either delegates to another constructor of the same class with `this(...)` or calls a parent constructor with `super(...)`. The compiler inserts `super()` only when neither is present, and only at the start of the chain. A cycle of `this(...)` calls does not compile. Keep the rules in the longest constructor and let the shorter ones chain into it, so one check covers every path into the class.

name: hook method
desc: An abstract method called from a final method in the parent. The parent fixes the skeleton, subclasses fill the gap.
body: A required step is `abstract`; an optional step is a concrete method with an empty body. Subclasses override only what they need. The `final` method in the parent is what turns this into a template: every subclass runs the same sequence, and a new step is added in one place. If a hook must return a value, give it a default rather than making it abstract, or every subclass pays for a step it does not use.

name: Interface.super.method()
desc: Picks one default method when a class implements two interfaces that declare the same signature.
body: The qualified form is legal only inside a class that implements the interface, and only for a direct superinterface. Outside the class there is no syntax for choosing a default method, which is the reason a conflict must be settled here rather than at the call site. If one interface already extends the other, the more specific default wins and the class needs no override.

name: static interface method
desc: Called on the interface name. Implementing classes do not inherit it, and it cannot be overridden.
body: A static interface method belongs to the interface, so `Payable.of(...)` works and `p.of(...)` does not compile. An implementing class may declare its own static method with the same name, and it hides instead of overrides, so the type in front of the dot decides which one runs. Use this for factories and validation helpers that belong with the contract but need no object state.

name: private interface method
desc: Java 9 and later. Shared code for default and static methods, invisible to implementing classes.
body: Before Java 9 the same helper had to be `public static`, which put it into the contract and into the documentation. A private method may also be static, and it may not be abstract. It exists only to stop two default methods from repeating a format, and it is the one member an implementing class cannot see at all.

name: sealed interface
syntax: sealed interface Name permits A, B { }
desc: Fixes the set of direct subtypes. Each permitted subtype must be final, sealed, or non-sealed.
body: A sealed type lists its direct subtypes, and they must sit in the same package, or the same module when a module descriptor is present. Each subtype then says what happens next: `final` stops the branch, `sealed` continues it with another list, `non-sealed` reopens it. The payoff is exhaustiveness: the compiler knows every subtype, so a switch over the sealed type needs no `default` and reports a missing case at build time.

name: switch pattern
desc: Tests the runtime type and binds a variable per arm. Over a sealed type the switch is exhaustive without a default.
body: Order matters: the guarded arm goes before the plain one, because the first match wins. A `null` value throws `NullPointerException` unless a `case null` arm exists. Over a type that is not sealed the compiler cannot prove exhaustiveness, so a `default` is required. Record patterns nest, so `case Wrapper(Bundle(int n, double f, boolean b))` reaches two levels in one line.

name: composition over inheritance
syntax: class A { private final B b; }
desc: Holds another object and calls it instead of extending it. One class, one reason to change.
body: The test is the is-a sentence. A booking is not a refund rule, so extending `RefundPolicy` would be wrong even when it saves typing. Composition keeps two axes apart: three booking kinds times three refund rules gives three subclasses when the rule is a field, and nine when the rule is a parent. A lambda often replaces the policy class entirely, which an abstract parent can never do.

name: covariant return type
desc: An override may return a subtype of the parent return type, so a caller through the child type skips the cast.
body: The return type may shrink, never widen, and never change to an unrelated type. This is why `Object.clone()` and many builder methods declare a subtype in their overrides. A parent typed variable still sees the parent return type, so the narrower type only removes a cast where the compiler can already prove the concrete class.
